subject: english-language
title: Marks that End Sentences
welcome_lead: Three little marks decide how a sentence ends.
meta_desc: KS3 English Language adventure on full stop, question and exclamation marks.
final_note: You can now choose the right sentence-end mark every time.

concepts.def: Opens a sentence; names a name.

walkthroughs.body_html: Use a full stop for statements; a question mark for questions; an exclamation mark for strong feeling or commands.
Capital letters start every sentence and mark proper nouns (names of people, places, brands).
'It rained.' — statement. 'Did it rain?' — question. 'Stop!' — exclamation/imperative. Each needs its own mark.

mcqs.q: What is overextension in child language?
options: Overextension is when children use very long words they don't understand.
When a child applies a word more broadly than adults do — e.g. calling all four-legged animals 'dog' before learning distinct categories.
Semantics is speech and pragmatics is writing.
Overextension is when children speak too loudly.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between semantics and pragmatics?
options: Semantics is speech and pragmatics is writing.
Overextension is when children speak too loudly.
Semantics is grammar and pragmatics is vocabulary.
Semantics studies literal meaning of words and sentences; pragmatics studies how meaning depends on context, speaker intention and conversational implicature.

mcqs.q: Are claims that women use more 'tentative' language well-supported?
options: Early studies (Lakoff) made broad claims, but later research (e.g. Holmes, Cameron) shows context matters more than gender, and many supposed differences disappear with proper data.
Women always use more hedges and tag questions than men.
Overextension is when children speak too loudly.
Women and men have different vocal cords so speak differently.
